content: The absence of calcium in the multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) may explain why certain dietary patterns were altered. When MNPs or small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) were included in the diet one to three days per week, the consumption of animal-source protein foods decreased. However, this reduction was not observed when Super Cereal Plus was included. When MNPs were included daily (seven days per week), there was a significant reduction in protein foods, reflecting that the iron target was met, and the Optifood model subsequently minimized protein intake. At nine months of age, MNPs only influenced dietary patterns when included daily, ensuring all target nutrient needs were met. In this scenario, vegetables were reduced, protein foods were nearly eliminated, and the intake of fruits, dairy, and added fats and oils increased. Including SQ-LNS daily reduced vegetable consumption, eliminated fruits, and minimized starchy staples to the lowest allowable levels. However, it did not significantly reduce protein foods for this age group, likely because iron needs were not fully met. Super Cereal Plus had minimal impact when included one or three days per week but reduced the intake of all other food groups when included daily. For nine-month-old infants, the inclusion of fortified items had the most significant impact on dietary patterns. Fortified items generally decreased starchy staples and increased fruit consumption in most scenarios. MNPs and SQ-LNS reduced animal-source protein foods and substantially increased added fats and oils while decreasing vegetable intake when included daily. In contrast, Super Cereal Plus eliminated dairy and reduced all other food groups except plant-based protein foods when included daily. MNPs increased dairy consumption, whereas other fortified items decreased it. For nine-month-old infants, fortified items increased the percentage of energy derived from fruits. MNPs and SQ-LNS reduced vegetable consumption, but Super Cereal Plus did not. The impact on dairy varied, with MNPs increasing dairy intake and both SQ-LNS and Super Cereal Plus decreasing it, particularly when included daily. Protein food intake showed slight increases in some scenarios, but the percentage of energy from protein foods remained low, reflecting the absence of nutrient gaps in this age group. Examples of weekly food patterns illustrate that dietary needs can be met with a variety of foods from different subgroups, depending on the specific items selected. For instance, a weekly pattern might include beef or sardines almost daily, small amounts of liver and tofu twice a week, and milk and cheese once a week. Quantities are approximate and based on weekly totals divided into standard serving sizes. Nutrient content in these examples may differ from modeled solutions, which use subgroup nutrient profiles. In real-world scenarios, diets in rural Bangladesh and Malawi were dominated by starchy staples, contributing 57–68% of energy from complementary foods. In contrast, Mexican diets had more moderate starchy staple consumption and higher intake of dairy and other animal-source foods. Compared to best-case patterns, diets in Bangladesh and Malawi had higher energy contributions from starchy staples, added fats, and unhealthy items, while energy from vegetables and animal-source protein foods was much lower. In Mexico, starchy staple consumption was similar to best-case levels during infancy but lower for non-breastfed children. Best-case scenarios for non-breastfed children showed very high energy contributions from starchy staples. Across all age groups, vegetable energy contributions were lower, while dairy energy contributions were higher. Protein energy contributions were lower during infancy but higher for non-breastfed children, as protein was minimized in best-case scenarios. Unhealthy items contributed significantly to energy intake for non-breastfed children in Mexico, accounting for 21% of total energy. Nutrient gaps were prevalent, particularly in Bangladesh and Malawi, where diets were deficient in several vitamins and minerals. Nutrient reference values (NRVs) were consistently met only for protein, alpha-linolenic acid, linoleic acid, vitamin A, vitamin C, and niacin equivalents. Iron and vitamin D levels were very low across all diets, and B vitamins and minerals were also below NRVs for some or all age groups in Bangladesh and Malawi. Mexican scenarios also showed deficiencies in several vitamins and minerals. Iron gaps were most effectively addressed by MNPs, followed by SQ-LNS, with Super Cereal Plus having a smaller impact. However, iron gaps remained significant in some scenarios, particularly with lower absorption assumptions. Zinc and copper upper limits (ULs) were sometimes exceeded, especially with daily SQ-LNS or MNPs. Feasible best-case food patterns were diverse, including 10–20 food subgroups per week, with diversity increasing with age and energy levels. Liberalized patterns allowed larger weekly quantities of each subgroup but remained diverse. These patterns included five to seven of the eight food groups in the WHO/UNICEF IYCF diversity indicator. For younger infants, patterns minimized starchy staples, providing only 4–5% of energy, and selected only whole-grain breakfast cereals. For older children, starchy staples contributed 24–26% of energy at moderate levels but increased to 37–38% for non-breastfed children at higher energy levels. Animal-source protein foods and diverse vegetable subgroups were included in all feasible patterns, with most also including plant-source protein foods. Fruits were included in all patterns except for the youngest infants, and small amounts of dairy were included in some patterns for breastfed infants and all patterns for non-breastfed infants. When iron absorption was assumed to be lower, significant iron gaps emerged for both breastfed and non-breastfed children, even in best-case patterns. These scenarios required higher protein energy contributions and lower carbohydrate energy contributions. Food patterns with lower absorption assumptions included more eggs and plant-based protein foods while reducing fruits. Modifications to food patterns often introduced additional nutrient gaps, particularly for the youngest age group with limited caloric availability for complementary foods. Eliminating food groups or subgroups, increasing staple food quantities, or introducing unhealthy items often resulted in new gaps for minerals and B vitamins. For example, removing vegetables introduced gaps for calcium, potassium, zinc, and magnesium, while eliminating dairy created a calcium gap. Patterns with monotonous staple foods, such as only roots/tubers or white rice, introduced gaps for calcium, potassium, zinc, and magnesium. Including unhealthy items displaced complementary foods and created gaps similar to those seen in scenarios with maximized staple foods. In summary, meeting nutrient needs for breastfed infants in this age group requires diverse diets with daily animal-source protein foods, ample and diverse vegetables, minimal starchy staples, and no refined grains or unhealthy items. Even in liberalized best-case scenarios, iron needs could not be fully met without fortified products. Fortified items, such as MNPs, SQ-LNS, or Super Cereal Plus, had varying effects on nutrient gaps depending on their composition and energy contribution. Daily MNPs eliminated the iron gap but introduced a magnesium gap due to minimized protein intake once all targets were met.
